texto: Let's get the obvious defense out of the way first, because you'll hear it from every critic who's ever taken a film theory 101 class: "Daniel Day-Lewis's performance is a towering achievement." Sure. It's also the film's biggest problem. A two-and-a-half-hour movie that survives entirely on the strength of one man's scenery-chewing is not a great film — it's a great audition tape wrapped in 158 minutes of your patience being tested. **The Pacing Is a Crime** Paul Thomas Anderson wants you to sit in silence. A lot. The opening fifteen minutes have no dialogue, which critics call "bold" and normal people call "a warning sign." This isn't tension-building — it's a director who fell in love with his own silences and forgot that atmosphere without momentum is just dead air with better cinematography. Entire scenes exist to communicate "time is passing" when a single title card would have done the job in half a second. You don't need to watch a man dig a hole for four minutes to understand that oil drilling is hard work. We get it. It's 1898. There's dirt. **Daniel Plainview Isn't a Character, He's a Costume** Plainview doesn't develop — he arrives fully formed as "bad" and spends the runtime getting worse in increasingly cartoonish ways, culminating in a finale so over-the-top it plays like parody of itself rather than tragedy. There's no arc here, just escalation. A character who starts as ruthless and ends as ruthless-but-louder isn't a study in the corrupting nature of capitalism — it's a flat line dressed up as a mountain range because the actor delivering it is loud enough to convince you something changed. "I drink your milkshake" isn't a chilling final gasp of a broken man; it's a meme that happened to occur inside a prestige film. **Eli Sunday Is a Cardboard Cutout** Paul Dano's Eli exists purely as a punching bag — literally, by the end — so that Plainview has something to dominate. He's not a real antagonist with competing logic; he's a strawman preacher built exclusively so the film can score cheap points against organized religion while congratulating itself for depth. Their rivalry has no texture, no give-and-take, just two men shouting past each other for two hours until one hits the other with a bowling pin. That's not a thematic payoff. That's a bar fight with a film degree. **The Score Is Doing the Emotional Labor the Script Won't** Jonny Greenwood's score gets credited with "unsettling dread," but strip it away and what you're left with is a script that mistakes vagueness for profundity. Scenes that feel important only feel that way because strings are screeching underneath them. Take away the music and half these "iconic" moments are just two men standing in a field not talking. **The Ending Doesn't Land — It Faceplants** "I'm finished" is supposed to be the exclamation point on a two-and-a-half-hour descent into moral rot. Instead, after 140 minutes of glacial restraint, the film suddenly sprints into full-blown melodrama, tonally severed from everything that came before it. It doesn't feel earned; it feels like Anderson ran out of ways to end the movie quietly and decided the loudest possible note would pass for "unforgettable." Loud isn't the same as earned. **Why Half a Star, Not Zero** Because the cinematography is genuinely good, and Day-Lewis, even in service of a thin character, is never boring to watch. That's it. That's the whole case for the other half star. Everything else — the pacing, the thematic shallowness dressed as depth, an antagonist with no interior life, a finale that abandons its own restraint — earns exactly what it gets: almost nothing.

Is there some way, some sufficiently grounded and authoritative image or line of dialogue, that could make this absence vivid, rather than asking the audience at a crucial moment to silently accept an allegorical mode of thought? There Will Be Blood es la película más sobrevalorada del siglo XXI. Para empezar, sus personajes están terriblemente escritos; son caricaturas sin verdadera profundidad. Tomemos como contraejemplo a David Fisher de Six Feet Under: es un hombre gay, pero también un ferviente creyente y conservador. Ambas facetas coexisten, dotándolo de complejidad. El personaje de Eli, por el contrario, es solo un patético y descarado estafador. Carece de esa hondura espiritual o contradicción interna que te permite empatizar con él, por muy terrible que sea. Por otro lado, la caricatura máxima es Daniel Plainview, un personaje con menos matices que Scrooge McDuck, el cual solo es un bufón que desea dinero (nadie sabe para qué) y poco más. Si el director quería retratar a los tiburones de la incipiente industria petrolera norteamericana, olvidó que estos hombres formaron enormes dinastías; no eran viejos huraños que acumulaban dinero para morir solos. Plainview parece una mezcla entre Charles Foster Kane y Ebenezer Scrooge, pero despojado de su humanidad y complejidad, quedándose solo con su lado más patético. Para colmo, tanto Paul Dano como Daniel Day-Lewis sobreactúan, lo que rompe cualquier atisbo de empatía. Paul Thomas Anderson los usa como personajes tesis (Religión vs. Capitalismo), pero se olvida de darles vida. El apartado técnico tampoco se salva. La música es una auténtica abominación que no encaja en absoluto con el ambiente. Es el equivalente a meterle música tecno a The Searchers o Lawrence of Arabia. La fotografía es buena, pero nada del otro mundo. Ese mismo año, No Country for Old Men o The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford presentaron trabajos infinitamente superiores. Además, se notan situaciones muy forzadas donde el director intenta pasarse de listo, como la pretenciosa ausencia de diálogos en ciertas escenas. La historia es minúscula, el conflicto apenas memorable y el guion parece un borrador mal hecho. Esto queda al desnudo en su patético final: un duelo intelectualoide que ni siquiera llega a serlo, donde el personaje de Dano no tiene réplica y solo lloriquea para que Plainview suelte un discurso nihilista digno de Reddit. Lo que queda, al final, es un monumento a la mediocridad.

A slow-paced film with stellar performances from Daniel Day-Lewis and Paul Dano. This film gets a low rating, not because it’s of poor quality, but due to the emotions it stirred within me. Personally, I believe that one of art’s purpose is to move us, emotionally, but sometimes the audience is ill-prepared for that experience. This film’s depiction of the Machiavellian dynamic between the protagonist and his adoptive son genuinely shocked me. Specifically, how the protagonist “disposed” of his adopted child once he became disabled. Seeing this has re-contextualized my relationship with my own adoptive family, and whether their love for me came from their altruism/benevolence or from a transactional benefit. Keeping it so real, I’m purposefully gonna be naive and delusionally subscribe to the former—I’m not emotionally ready to process what came out of this Pandora’s box. The diner scene from the film Beautiful Boy (2018) is the only other media to make me feel this way. I’ll come back to this film and reassess in a few years once I’ve processed my childhood trauma.

There Will Be Blood - Raved about, but maybe little true quality Entertainment I came late to this movie and found it almost humorous to see ‘critics’ claiming that this picture offers a serious commentary on capitalism and greed inherent in American society. Greed has been with us forever, but ‘Capitalism’ might be a bit of a long bow to draw. The critics of capitalism will mainly come from communist run countries, where the state takes all and gives you what ‘they’ think you should get – not much room for freedom of choice there. At least under capitalism, everyone has the choice to progress, and that progress can be shared with the broader population. Capitalism also establishes rules to curb greed (even though corrupt individuals seek to circumvent them), but that same greed exists in many communist-run nations.  It’s also rather doubtful that this adapter/filmmaker had this theme in mind when initially embarking on this project. As with other works by previously self-confessed drug and porn addicted P.T. Anderson, insanity is never far away from his central characters. And capitalism does not exist or develop simply from insanity alone; it’s also a creation often used for the greater good of the community, but rarely in today’s democratic Hollywood will we see this being touted. Anderson, like Tarantino, employs ideas ‘borrowed’ from other great works, and the first 150 pages he’s adapted from Upton Sinclair’s epic novel ‘Oil’ may bear little resemblance to this pastiche. Daniel Day-Lewis’ at times over-the-top portrayal is more the product of a performer immersing himself into the writer’s peculiar character than the result of truly great ‘acting’. As others have noted, he went about the set being as unhinged as the character he was portraying, long after the cameras stopped rolling. The final preposterous scenes of mayhem and blood totally destroy any claims to greatness and leave this as just another P.T.A. overindulgence for clickbait critics to bestow their rave reviews.  Yes, cinematically it looks good, but perhaps when thought about after the fact, we can most certainly find better things to let fester in our heads. For fans only. As a footnote, I can only agree with several critical evaluations that dared to speak out, such as: Carla Meyer: who concluded,  "It's perhaps the one most inflated with its own delusional self-importance". Roger Ebert:  "There Will Be Blood is the kind of film that is easily called great. I am not sure of its greatness. There Will Be Blood is not perfect, and in its imperfections, its ending (its relentlessness), we may see its reach exceeding its grasp. Mick LaSalle:  challenged the film's high praise by saying "there should be no need to pretend There Will Be Blood is a masterpiece just because Anderson sincerely tried to make it one" and noting that "the scenes between Day-Lewis and Dano ultimately degenerate into a ridiculous burlesque."

Clearest example of a movie which thinks it's far deeper than it actually is. Perhaps the biggest flaw is that the movie plays it's cards way too early. Instead of being a slow unravel of DDL's character from a simple man just capitalising upon opportunity to make profit into a slimeball who will sell his own family for money, it starts with the premise that DDL is a slimeball who ends up being a murderous slimeball by the end. There remains no proper character arc for him, it's just him being a bigger and bigger dick to everyone. Therefore, his ultimate descent into madness, while convincing, just doesn't seem all that surprising. There's also the problem that fundamentally, we don't understand why DDL is a money hungry slimeball because the movie starts off with that premise as is. Yes, capitalism corrupts him, but he already was pretty corrupt from the get go. This difference between what his arc is, and what it was supposed to be, breaks the film for me. Secondly, it's just plain boring in places. Having seen this and One Battle after Another, I understand that PTA isn't exactly a filmmaker with a tight script, which is fine. However, the film overindulges itself, there is so much content that doesn't have an adequate payoff, or contributes zilch to the overall narrative (except for maybe hammering home that DDL is truly evil, but that was literally the first point the movie made). Therefore, the movie meanders a lot and whatever steam it occassionally picks up is immediately lost. It also has an abrupt ending with no rhyme or rhythm to it. To me, it seems very evident that PTA had no clue how to truly end the movie. None of that is to discredit DDL's performance however, who plays the role of the smooth talking smarmy bastard so well I was actually second guessing his intentions for a long time. It also explains why he's won 3 Oscars.

Si algo me ha enseñado el arte es que no hay mejor forma de explorar la condición humana que con los matices, y por esto es que no puedo ser fan de esta película. Verán, esta película nos plantea a sus dos personajes principales como “dos caras de una misma moneda” y el final (que no me gustó) como Daniel destruyendo a su propio reflejo, cuando, según lo que muestra, no es el caso, haciendo que el punto de la película se sienta empujado por el director. ¿Por qué digo esto? Verán, La Biblia y la teología están redactadas de tal forma que cualquier duda ellos buscan una forma de procesarla, tipo: si algo sale mal, es una prueba; si dudas, te faltó fe; si te atacan, es el enemigo, etc., etc. Eli no tenía las herramientas emocionales ni intelectuales para cuestionar eso. Para él, actuar como un profeta y buscar sanar a la gente no era un fraude; ponerlo como la cara de una moneda de alguien mucho más intencionado y manipulador no es una comparación justa. En la película se nos menciona el tema del maltrato (jamás lo elaboraron, solo lo mencionaron) hacia Mary, la hermana de Eli, por parte de su padre cuando ella no quiere rezar, por lo cual uno asume que lo mismo le pasaba a Eli, lo cual incluso lo convierte en una víctima, diría yo; una víctima que se convierte en victimario, pero una víctima al final del día. ¿Entienden mi punto? Compararlo con un misántropo multimillonario y sin escrúpulos como Daniel y pretender que pensemos que es una pelea de iguales no funciona. Al querer forzar la tesis, no hay nada de neutralidad, ni una exploración más a fondo de la fe, no hay nada de matices aquí, y por ende tampoco esperanza, ni una solución, ni personas decentes, haciéndola, para mí, muuuuy pesada y aburrida. Y no estoy pidiendo que la película defienda la religión; si quería el director enfrentar a Daniel y Eli como dos fuerzas opuestas, habría sido mucho más interesante mostrar con mayor profundidad qué significa la fe para Eli y para la comunidad, en lugar de utilizar principalmente la religión como un conflicto. Y sobre H.W., desde el inicio nos mostraron que lo veía como una extensión de él mismo, por eso hasta le daba alcohol, bien hasta ahí, por eso entiendo que se sienta traicionado, ¿pero que le diga que nunca lo quiso? 🤦‍♂️ ¿ven mi problema? Esta película siempre busca que los personajes se vuelvan más oscuros, pero de una forma que parece que pasa porque así lo quiere el director y no porque sean contradicciones humanas. Por eso odié tanto el final, no solo porque la pelea me parezca mal coreografiada, ni porque me pareció ridícula en comparación de la seriedad del resto de la película, sino también porque dejó varias cosas inconclusas y un mensaje muy limitado. No la volvería a ver, me aburrí.

There Will Be Blood is one of those movies where I can absolutely understand why people think it’s great, while also admitting that it just didn’t really work for me. Daniel Day-Lewis is incredible. There’s no getting around that. His performance is intense, strange, intimidating, and easily the most memorable part of the entire movie. He completely owns every scene he’s in. The problem is that the movie itself felt way too slow for me. There are long stretches where very little seems to happen, and while I understand the movie is more interested in character, obsession, greed, and power than traditional plot, I still found myself losing interest. There are definitely some great moments, and the tension between the characters can be excellent when the movie decides to really lean into it. But getting from one of those moments to the next felt like work. I respect the performances, the filmmaking, and what the movie is trying to do. I just can’t say I particularly enjoyed watching it. A technically impressive movie with an incredible lead performance, but far too slow to keep me fully invested.

Una costante nei racconti di cinema di Paul Thomas Anderson è senza dubbio quella di applicare l’istantanea di un determinato tempo cronologico a ciò che fa vedere allo spettatore. L’America di un segmento storico preciso che rispecchia la sua storia in ogni sua forma, incarnandone i luoghi, i costumi, le abitudini e l’aspetto sociale che comprende il periodo. L’affresco culturale nel film del 2007 “Il petroliere” rappresenta l’immagine della caccia all’oro nero di fine Ottocento, che ha come protagonista indiscusso Daniel Plainview, interpretato dal tre volte premio Oscar Daniel Day-Lewis. Tra l’altro, questa performance lo porterà proprio alla vittoria della prestigiosa statuetta. Daniel Plainview e la fame di potere La narrazione di un cacciatore di petrolio spregiudicato, che erge un’impresa a conduzione familiare, composta soltanto da lui e il suo bambino come socio. In questa pellicola alcune figure cercano di spiccare con lineamenti differenti, ma tutti hanno un solo unico obiettivo velato nella testa: arricchirsi. Le oltre due ore e mezza del film spiegheranno che i mezzi per arrivare al traguardo, per alcuni, contano fino a un certo punto, ma spesso bisogna fare i conti con chi i conti li ha saputi fare e mettere in pratica, oppure ha saputo muoversi in anticipo e con maggiore astuzia. Così Daniel è disposto a tutto pur di trivellare terreni per ottenere petrolio: anche disfarsi di un figlio o rinfacciargli l’amara verità delle sue sfasate origini, e scoprire una messa in scena utile per il fine. Allo stesso modo, c’è chi usa la parola di Dio per i suoi scopi, per poi rinnegarla se necessario al momento opportuno, al limite fingersi un parente di qualcuno più vicino alla ricchezza per trarne beneficio. Ma il tempo finisce sempre per rivelare il trucco, svelando e premiando solo chi ha saputo giocare bene le sue carte e prendersi tutto. “Voglio guadagnare così tanto da stare lontano da tutti.” Isolamento, violenza e spirito del West Daniel farà terra bruciata intorno a lui, cercando di non farsi fregare da chi vorrebbe la sua torta senza il sudore della fronte, oppure da chi vorrebbe mangiarsi anche solo una fetta. Questa avida guerra personale contro chiunque tende ad isolare l’individuo, spronandolo a togliere di mezzo chi prova a fregarlo o mettersi di traverso, senza fare prigionieri. Perché in queste ultime battute western lo spirito del selvaggio West non sbiadisce alla nuova fame di ricchezza economica: tende a divampare nell’uomo disposto a scannarsi per i propri affari e tutto ciò che ha in tasca, senza dividerlo con nessuno. “Io guardo le persone e non ci trovo niente di attraente. Io vedo il peggio delle persone.” Tecnica e nichilismo La storia scorre attraverso tecnicismi da pellicola impeccabili, dall’ottima fotografia ad aspetti narrativi che immergono lo spettatore nel contesto, sbattuto in faccia già soltanto grazie alle espressioni del protagonista, che per larghi tratti iniziali non ha bisogno neanche di parlare. Passando per alcuni monologhi di cortesia davanti alla comunità, fino a discorsi serrati e psichedelici che buttano fuori il proprio essere, immagazzinato e nascosto insieme allo spietato egoismo che si cela dietro un classico volto di uomo d’affari. Il successo del nichilismo sta tutto nella cinicità famelica del protagonista, che smonta la filosofia di ogni suo antagonista, svestendolo fino all’ultima goccia di sangue e confermando il capitalismo come sola e unica vera dottrina del tempo.

Je ne pensais pas être capable de haïr le capitalisme encore plus. Pis là je me suis rappelé que le capitalisme est un jeu d'hommes orgueilleux et égocentriques. Pis, avant que je tombe dans l'analyse, wow. Daniel Day-Lewis a donné une des meilleures performances que j'ai jamais vues par un homme dans l'histoire hollywoodienne. On sentait une rage intense, une peur profonde, une grande confusion et une immense violence canalisée. C'est le genre de jeu d'acteur que les gens essayent d'associer à Robert de Niro. Je crois aussi que la limite de l'expression qu'il présente n'est pas due à son jeu d'acteur, mais au personnage. C'est un homme de violence et, en ce sens, Day-Lewis incarne le personnage avec une immense exactitude. Venant d'un historien, j'aime beaucoup l'écriture de ce film. On comprend que c'est une critique du capitalisme et du Rêve. Daniel incarne le "self-made man". L'homme qui s'est enivré d'une idée de grandeur en ignorant la petitesse de ses valeurs. Le choix de la période de prospection et du développement des pipelines dans le sud californien fin XIXe, début XXe, est incroyablement pertinente. C'est la période la plus importante dans la formation de l'imaginaire culturel américain. Certes, il s'ancre dans une tradition d'américanité digne de l'Almanach du Petit Richard, mais il s'incruste bien dans le fantasmagorique univers du début d'Hollywood. On est en train de créer les archétypes. On voit à l'écran les balbutiements du Cow-Boy et de l'Indien, la création du cinéma de foi, le lancement du cinéma historique et militaire. Bref, on est à la genèse de l'image. Et le film propose de briser cette image contemporaine. Elle présente un homme rapaillé qui s'est perdu dans un rêve d'or noir. Une figure qui est en discorde profonde avec le capitalisme de gentlemen rockerfelleriste, et le pionnier du Manifest Destiny. C'est une attaque directe à la fondation même de ce sur quoi se repose le rêve américain actuel. "I am the Third Revelation" Daniel hurle de manière injurieuse à Eli, un pasteur, alors qu'il lui garnotte des boules de bowling et lui fissure le crâne avec une quille. L'homme qui est si riche qu'il peut acheter la croyance. Un écho sanglant de Nietzsche sous la forme bien imagée que Dieu est mort dans le sang noir d'un nouveau système de croyance prépondérant à la finalité divine. On voit dieu comme un service, une utilité pour la conscience. La personne qui considère que le profit est l'outil de l'Église se fait laisser giser pour mort sur une allée de quille bien cirée. La morale chrétienne a formé une grande partie des normes criminelles du XXe siècle. C'est une réalité sociale, mais aussi individuelle. Lorsque l'on comprend le personnage troublé de Daniel Plainview, on comprend une violence capitale subséquente à la morale aveugle. There Will Be Blood was a very interesting movie that, at first, I thought I was going to dislike. The beginning started off quite slow and was beginning to lose my attention, but the sudden graphic deaths throughout the film surprised me and immediately pulled me back in. I almost rated it three stars, but after seeing the ending, I finally understood what Eli Sunday and Daniel Plainview represented. The writing of their relationship, and the eventual reversal of their roles, was very well done. Earlier in the film, Eli saves and baptizes Daniel with water, calling it the “blood of Christ.” By the end, Daniel is surrounded by his own “blood of Christ” in the form of alcohol, which Eli also gives in to. The conclusion, with Daniel killing Eli after Eli had once “saved” him, was an ending I did not expect and made me appreciate the film much more.

I genuinely thought Eli was just gonna have a one sided beef with Daniel, turns out they’re both just as greedy for power and money, literally two sides of the same coin. And I guess capitalism won, Daniel ended up getting what he wanted but at what cost… he wasn’t very happy To be honest I had low expectations, not because of the production, performance or anything related to the film, but because of me. I thought I wouldn’t like it, but it was awesome, I truly enjoyed watching it. There Will Be Blood: El Choque de los Falsos Profetas There Will Be Blood (2007) no es únicamente una obra cumbre del cine contemporáneo; es un monumento de una belleza sobrecogedora sobre la ambición, la fe y la oscuridad sobre la que se erigió la modernidad. Paul Thomas Anderson no se limita a filmar el nacimiento de un imperio petrolero, sino la génesis de una devoción destructiva. A través de una dirección magistral y de un pulso estético formidable, Anderson construye un poema trágico donde la tierra, el petróleo y la sangre se funden en una sola sustancia negra que devora todo a su paso. En el plano técnico, la cámara de Anderson se mueve con la autoridad de los grandes clásicos, regalando composiciones donde la inmensidad desértica de Texas contrasta con la pequeñez de los hombres que la profanan . La fotografía de Robert Elswit aprovecha la luz natural para abrazar la pantalla con tonos dorados y secos en el exterior, mientras enmarca los interiores en una penumbra envolvente iluminada a fuego. Todo este despliegue visual se entrelaza de forma hipnótica con la atonal y disonante música de Jonny Greenwood, una partitura de cuerdas percutidas que no busca decorar la imagen, sino hacer retumbar el crujido interno de una máquina a punto de colapsar. Más allá de su forma imponente, la película se sostiene sobre una trama devastadora que funciona como una colisión de fuerzas primarias. Anderson nos adentra en la historia de dos hombres obsesionados con el control, cuyas vidas quedan entrelazadas por un mismo veneno: la necesidad enfermiza de dominación. Por un lado, Daniel Plainview —encarnado por un titánico Daniel Day-Lewis— representa el deseo irracional de acumular tanto poder que le permita aislarse por completo de la humanidad. Del otro lado, Eli Sunday —un extraordinario Paul Dano— viste esa misma sed de poder bajo el ropaje de la fe. No son antagonistas convencionales; son las dos caras de una misma moneda, dos fanáticos empujados por el mismo vacío. La psique de Daniel Plainview es un abismo fascinante y aterrador. Su ambición no busca el lujo ni el reconocimiento social; nace de un odio visceral y patológico hacia sus semejantes, una misantropía que él mismo confiesa al admitir que contempla a las personas y no encuentra nada en ellas que le guste. Para Daniel, el mundo es un campo de batalla donde solo existen dos posturas: dominar o ser dominado. Su megalomanía lo empuja a competir hasta con el aire que respira, convirtiendo cada interacción humana en una transacción de poder donde la empatía es una debilidad inaceptable. Esa paranoia y ese egoísmo feroz terminan por envenenar los únicos vínculos de sangre que podrían haberlo salvado de la abyección. A su hijo adoptivo, H.W., lo utiliza inicialmente como una simpática herramienta de negocios para proyectar la falsa imagen de un hombre de familia; pero en cuanto el pequeño pierde la audición en un accidente en la torre de extracción, la incapacidad de Daniel para gestionar la fragilidad ajena lo lleva a abandonarlo en un tren, prefiriendo la frialdad del petróleo a la responsabilidad del amor filial. De la misma forma, cuando aparece en su vida un hombre que afirma ser su hermano, Daniel experimenta un efímero destello de vulnerabilidad, buscando desesperadamente un refugio emocional. Sin embargo, al descubrir la mentira, su furia cobra la vida del impostor, cerrando herméticamente la última puerta que le quedaba hacia la compasión. Ese patrón de desprecio culmina años después en la ruptura definitiva con H.W., ya como un hombre adulto. Cuando su hijo acude a informarle que desea casarse y abrir su propia compañía petrolera en México, Daniel reacciona con una mezquindad aterradora: se niega en redondo a comunicarse a través del intérprete de lenguaje de señas, rechazando frontalmente el puente que la discapacidad de su hijo exige para encontrarse. En lugar de celebrar la independencia del joven, la ambición y la neurosis de Daniel interpretan ese deseo de emancipación como una traición comercial. Es en ese diálogo donde el padre destruye lo último que quedaba del vínculo, revelándole a sangre fría que no es su hijo verdadero, sino un huérfano recogido del fango para dar una cara amable a sus negocios. La marcha en silencio de H.W. y la risa grotesca de Daniel al quedarse solo en su salón enmarcan la verdadera tragedia de la película: la amputación voluntaria del amor filial, donde el padre prefiere quedarse en la absoluta ruina afectiva antes que ceder un ápice de su orgullo. La relación entre Plainview y Eli es un baile de máscaras donde la religión y el dinero compiten por doblegar al otro. Su enfrentamiento alcanza una dimensión casi poética cuando se examina la evolución de su odio: dos rituales de humillación que se responden a lo largo de los años como un espejo deformante. La famosa secuencia en la iglesia, donde Daniel se somete al bautismo para lograr sus objetivos comerciales, no es un acto de fe, sino una derrota física fingida para salvaguardar sus intereses. Sin embargo, la herida en el orgullo del magnate queda abierta, madurando en silencio hasta transformarse en una promesa de venganza que tardará décadas en cobrar la factura. Cuando el tiempo pasa y la historia nos traslada al clímax en la bolera, el ajuste de cuentas no es una cuestión de dinero ni de tierras; es la destrucción absoluta de la dignidad. Plainview exige la rendición espiritual de su rival no por necesidad, sino por el puro placer de ver desmoronarse el altar sobre el que Eli construyó su vida. La confrontación final es la puesta en escena de dos almas que han vendido todo lo que tenían para terminar encontrándose en un espacio cerrado, frío y desolado, donde la victoria de uno significa la consumación de la tragedia de ambos. Es en ese instante donde la película regala uno de los cierres más rotundos y memorables de la historia del cine. Tras consumar la destrucción de su enemigo, un Daniel exhausto y roto sentencia con un hilo de voz: "I'm finished". Esa línea de diálogo es una daga de doble filo: marca el final de su venganza, pero también certifica la muerte de su propia humanidad. Plainview ha ganado la batalla y ha conquistado el subsuelo, pero se ha quedado completamente solo en el vacío de su imperio. There Will Be Blood es el triunfo del cine como arte mayor; una exploración apasionada e inolvidable de cómo la ambición desmedida no construye un futuro, sino un desierto en el alma.

“I have a competition in me. I want no one else to succeed. I hate most people.” | “I see the worst in people, Henry. I don't need to look past seeing them to get all I need. I've built up my hatreds over the years, little by little.” The film is without a shadow of a doubt a masterpiece, one of the best pieces of film I have ever seen and for sure top 5 of the 21st century. Now I view the whole thing as power-struggle between Daniel (representing business) vs. Eli (representing religion), and whose method of controlling people for their own benefit is more effective. From Daniel's perspective, he absolutely hates Eli because he views him as a charlatan/showman, whereas he is actually producing something of "value" by actively engaging in economic competition. Of course, his lack of spirituality, ethics, and morality ultimately results in Daniel literally isolating himself in his mansion and disowning his adopted son, but from the perspective of the character, he accomplishes absolutely everything he sets out to do. More broadly speaking, I think you can view Daniel representing something like Nietzsche's Ubermensch. The general criticisms of religion and capitalism are fairly self-evident, but I believe the film is largely a character-study of Daniel Plainview and the late-19th/early 20th-century robber barons he is meant to represent. I can't think of too many films that are deconstructions of religion and capitalism/industrialism well, while also managing not to be condescending, yet are simultaneously entertaining and intelligent character studies. It's a unique film in this regard, and I doubt PTA ever makes a better one. Daniel Plainview is such a magnificent deep character and there is so much I can say about him, Daniel Day-Lewis made a superb work, perfect dare I say, and has so many layers, its almost impossible to cover them all. The crippling loneliness Plainview lives in is his only humanizing feature to me. The other characters, even those close to him, never understand who he is and his utter isolation is heartbreaking. His attempt to reach out to his "brother" show us the only time he lets down his guard in an effort to find some sort of understanding in himself. That said I don't think he sees the worst in people but instead sees himself in them. As he hates himself and his life, his greed and self-absorption make him project hatred towards other people. I think he hated the idea of being a bad father, like his own before him, and projected this hatred onto the Standard Oil representatives. The same can be said about Eli, he is dumb, weak, malicious, and uses the pretext of faith to lure people to his benefit. As Plainview drains oil, so is his humanity drained by his hatred of his never-satisfied life. That revelation on that beach was absolutely a terrific piece of filmography. Great camera shot and acting. You can totally see him put the pieces together, it's great. Side point to say that I don’t even undestand how can Tarantino criticize Paul Dano in this. He was playing a weak man so well, Tarantino thought he was a weak actor, and I think what’s most important is that it takes a strong actor to play a weak man, especially as great as Dano does it.
